projects.desc: A lightweight session manager for git worktrees. Grove tracks your active branches, keeps each worktree tidy, and lets you hop between parallel tasks without context-switching chaos.

pages.title: Grove Overview
pages.body:
# Grove Overview

Grove is a lightweight session manager for git worktrees. It tracks your active
branches, keeps each worktree tidy, and lets you hop between parallel tasks
without context-switching chaos.

## Why Grove

Working several branches at once usually means stashing, checking out, and
losing your place. Grove gives each task its **own worktree and tmux session**,
so switching is instant and nothing leaks between tasks.

## How a session flows

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Session submitted] --> B["bind_tools()"]
    B --> C[Create worktree]
    C --> D[Start tmux session]
    D --> E[Run agent loop]
    E --> F{Done?}
    F -- no --> E
    F -- yes --> G[Prune worktree]
```

## At a glance

- `grove create <branch>` provisions an isolated workspace.
- `grove list` shows every active worktree and its status.
- `grove peek <id>` prints a bounded snapshot without attaching.
- `grove kill <id>` tears the workspace down and prunes the worktree.

Grove is pure Python and needs no daemon for the core flow; a small optional
daemon exposes the same operations over HTTP.

pages.title: Runtime Model
pages.body:
# Runtime Model

Grove's runtime is a thin coordinator around three long-lived resources: the
**workspace store**, a **git runner**, and a **tmux adapter**. Nothing is global
— every operation resolves the workspace it targets, then delegates to a
collaborator injected at construction.

## The core loop

A running workspace is an agent process inside a tmux session. Grove itself does
not drive the agent; it provisions the environment, records the mapping, and
gets out of the way. State transitions (`active`, `paused`, `killed`) are
recorded on the workspace record, never inferred from tmux.

```python
ws = store.create(branch="feature/login")
tmux.start(ws.session, cwd=ws.worktree)
store.mark(ws.id, "active")
```

## Why a coordinator, not a daemon

The core flow is synchronous and local: create a worktree, start a session,
record it. Keeping that daemonless means `grove` works over SSH with no server
to babysit. The optional daemon reuses the exact same coordinator behind an
HTTP surface.

pages.title: Workspace Store
pages.body:
# Workspace Store

The workspace store is the single source of truth for which branch maps to which
worktree and which tmux session. It is a small, append-friendly record set keyed
by a stable workspace id.

## Record shape

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | stable short id (the tmux session name) |
| `branch` | the branch checked out in the worktree |
| `worktree` | absolute path under the grove root |
| `status` | `active`, `paused`, or `killed` |

## Guarantees

- A branch maps to **at most one** live worktree; creating a second reuses the
  first.
- The record is written **before** the worktree exists and updated after, so a
  crash mid-create is recoverable by `grove prune`.
- `kill` marks the record and removes the worktree in one step, so the store and
  the filesystem never drift.

pages.title: Session Lifecycle
pages.body:
# Session Lifecycle

Every workspace moves through a small, explicit lifecycle. Grove never guesses a
state from tmux or the filesystem — each transition is an operation that writes
the store first.

## States

- **create** — reserve a record, add the worktree, start the tmux session.
- **pause** — detach the agent and mark the record `paused`; the worktree stays.
- **resume** — reattach and mark `active`.
- **kill** — stop the session, prune the worktree, mark `killed`.

## Cleanup

Killing a workspace tears down the tmux session and runs `git worktree prune`,
leaving the repository exactly as it was before the task started. Orphaned
worktrees (from an interrupted create) are reclaimed by `grove prune`, which
reconciles the store against `git worktree list`.

pages.title: CLI Reference
pages.body:
# CLI Reference

Grove is driven entirely from the `grove` command. Every verb resolves a
workspace, then delegates to the runtime.

## Verbs

| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `grove create <branch>` | provision an isolated worktree + tmux session |
| `grove list` | list active workspaces and their status |
| `grove peek <id>` | print a bounded status snapshot |
| `grove attach <id>` | attach to the workspace's tmux session |
| `grove pause <id>` | detach and mark the workspace paused |
| `grove resume <id>` | reattach a paused workspace |
| `grove kill <id>` | stop the session and prune the worktree |
| `grove prune` | reconcile the store against `git worktree list` |

## Example

```console
$ grove create feature/login
created ws-7f3a  ->  .grove/feature-login  (tmux: ws-7f3a)
$ grove list
ws-7f3a  active   feature/login
```

pages.title: Configuration
pages.body:
# Configuration

Grove reads an optional `grove.toml` from the repository root, falling back to
sensible defaults so it works with zero configuration.

## Keys

```toml
[grove]
root = ".grove"          # where worktrees are created
naming = "branch-slug"    # how session ids are derived
default_shell = "zsh"     # shell started inside each tmux session

[hooks]
post_create = "direnv allow"
pre_kill = "git status --porcelain"
```

## Precedence

Configuration resolves lowest-to-highest: built-in defaults, then `grove.toml`,
then any `GROVE_*` environment variable. A missing file is not an error — the
defaults are the documented behaviour.

pages.title: Git & Tmux
pages.body:
# Git & Tmux

Grove's isolation rests on two primitives it never abstracts away: **git
worktrees** for filesystem isolation and **tmux sessions** for process
isolation.

## Worktrees

Each workspace is created with `git worktree add <path> <branch>`, pinned to its
own branch under the grove root. Because worktrees share the object store but
not the working tree, two tasks can build against the same repository without a
shared index.

## Tmux

A tmux session named for the workspace holds the agent process. Switching tasks
is a `tmux switch-client`, not a `git checkout` — your place in each task is
preserved exactly. Grove shells out through a small adapter so the tmux calls are
testable without a live server.

## Teardown

`kill` runs `git worktree remove` and `git worktree prune`, then kills the tmux
session, so neither git nor tmux is left holding a dead reference.

pages.title: Contributor Workflow
pages.body:
# Contributor Workflow

Grove is small on purpose. The contributor loop is: fork a worktree with Grove
itself, make the change, run the suite, open a PR.

## Setup

```console
$ uv sync --all-extras --all-groups
$ grove create feature/my-change
$ grove attach ws-...
```

## Conventions

- One atomic class per feature; collaborators injected as fields.
- Tests prefer real code paths and stub only the git/tmux subprocess boundary.
- Commit messages follow Gitmoji + Conventional Commits.

## Tests

`pytest` runs the full suite. The git and tmux adapters are the only I/O seams,
so most tests inject fakes and never touch a real repository or server.

pages.title: Architecture
pages.body:
# Architecture

Grove layers cleanly: a **CLI** on top, a **runtime coordinator** in the middle,
and three injected collaborators — the **store**, the **git runner**, and the
**tmux adapter** — at the bottom.

## Dependency flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CLI --> Runtime
    Runtime --> Store
    Runtime --> Git
    Runtime --> Tmux
```

Dependencies flow strictly downward. The runtime never imports the CLI, and the
collaborators never import the runtime — each is constructed and injected, which
is what makes the runtime testable without a shell.

## The daemon

The optional daemon is a thin HTTP surface over the *same* runtime. It hosts no
logic of its own; it composes the coordinator exactly as the CLI does, so the
two front ends can never drift.

pages.title: Daemon API
pages.body:
# Daemon API

The optional `groved` daemon exposes Grove's operations over HTTP for tools that
can't shell out. It is a thin transport over the same runtime the CLI uses.

## Endpoints

| Method | Path | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/workspaces` | list active workspaces |
| `POST` | `/workspaces` | create a workspace for a branch |
| `GET` | `/workspaces/{id}` | a bounded status snapshot |
| `POST` | `/workspaces/{id}/pause` | pause a workspace |
| `DELETE` | `/workspaces/{id}` | kill and prune |

## Contract

Request and response bodies are strict, validated models — an unknown field is a
clean `400`, never a silent no-op. The daemon owns transport only; every state
transition still goes through the runtime coordinator.

projects.desc: AI assistant with a built-in agent hypervisor. Spawns, scopes, and manages parallel sub-agents across tasks.

pages.title: Project Overview
pages.body:
# Project Overview

Mewbo is an AI assistant modelled as a **conversation state machine** with a
hierarchical **agent hypervisor**. A single async tool-use loop is bound to an
LLM via native `bind_tools`; sub-agents are admitted through `spawn_agent` and
resolved into one of four terminal states.

## What it does

- Runs an agentic loop over your own tools, with strict validated contracts at
  every trust boundary.
- Spawns, scopes, and manages **parallel sub-agents** across tasks.
- Exposes the one engine through the CLI, web console, REST API, Home Assistant,
  and Nextcloud Talk.

## Where to go next

The **Agentic Search Engine** and **Source Capability Graph** pages cover
retrieval; the **Mewbo API Server** page covers the HTTP surface.

pages.title: Agentic Search Engine
pages.body:
# Agentic Search Engine

Agentic Search answers a question by fanning probes across saved multi-source
workspaces, then returning a **cited** answer plus the results it drew from.

## Flow

1. A search run spins up its own session and a fleet of probe leaves.
2. Each probe records an `access` event per retrieval call.
3. A finalizer folds the accesses into a bounded, ranked provenance trail.

The root agent holds no retrieval tools of its own — it orchestrates the
probes and synthesises the cited answer.

pages.title: Source Capability Graph (SCG)
pages.body:
# Source Capability Graph (SCG)

The SCG is a **reachability engine**: given a task, it routes to the capability
(a tool, a connector, a source) most likely to satisfy it. The store is global
per source — flat, content-addressed node ids — and a workspace is a scoped
*view*, never a copy.

## Routing

A cheap router scores candidate recipes over `cosine + edge` and can blend a
memory-bias term, all with **zero LLM** on the hot path. Out-of-scope
candidates are dropped by the ambient scope, so per-source mappings stay shared
while insights stay workspace-isolated.

pages.title: Channels & Integrations
pages.body:
# Channels & Integrations

Every interface shares the same core engine — only the transport differs.

| Channel | Surface |
| --- | --- |
| CLI | Rich/Textual terminal app |
| Web console | React + shadcn console |
| REST API | Flask-RESTX server |
| Home Assistant | conversation agent |
| Nextcloud Talk | chat bridge |

Because the engine is one library the channels compose, a capability added once
is available everywhere without per-channel glue.

pages.title: Mewbo API Server
pages.body:
# Mewbo API Server

The API server is a thin shell: HTTP routes, SSE framing, run/job lifecycle, and
persistence glue. The reusable engine and domain models live in the libraries it
composes — it never re-hosts an engine.

## Contracts

Anything crossing a trust boundary — tool arguments, request bodies, persisted
documents — is a strict Pydantic model with `extra="forbid"`, so a smuggled
field is a clean `400`, not a silent no-op.

pages.title: Agent Hypervisor
pages.body:
# Agent Hypervisor

The hypervisor tracks every spawned sub-agent and resolves it into exactly one
terminal state: `completed`, `failed`, `cancelled`, or `rejected`. It owns
admission (`spawn_agent`), accounting, and teardown.

## Why a hypervisor

A flat loop can't reason about a tree of concurrent agents. The hypervisor makes
the tree explicit, so scoping, cancellation, and attribution are first-class
rather than emergent.

pages.title: Tool-Use Loop
pages.body:
# Tool-Use Loop

The core engine is a single async `ToolUseLoop` bound to an LLM. Each turn: the
model proposes tool calls, the loop validates and runs them, and the results
feed the next turn until the task completes.

## Normalisation

Cross-model tool-calling differences are handled at the LiteLLM/adapter seam —
never by sniffing text format inside the loop — so the orchestration stays model
agnostic.

projects.desc: A feature-flag and remote-config service: typed flags, attribute targeting, and stable percentage rollouts.

pages.title: Overview
pages.body:
# Beacon

Beacon is a **feature-flag and remote-config service**. It stores typed flags,
evaluates them against a caller-supplied context, and serves the result to
application SDKs over a small HTTP API.

## At a glance

- Flags are typed: boolean, string, integer, or JSON.
- Every evaluation is a pure function of `(flag, context)` — no hidden state.
- Clients cache the ruleset locally and re-evaluate offline.

pages.title: Flag Model
pages.body:
# Flag Model

A flag is a named, typed value plus an ordered list of rules. The first rule
whose predicate matches wins; if none match, the flag's default value is
returned.

```json
{
  "key": "checkout.new-basket",
  "type": "boolean",
  "default": false,
  "rules": [
    { "when": { "plan": "enterprise" }, "value": true }
  ]
}
```

A flag's `type` is immutable once created — changing it would silently break
every SDK that already decoded the old type.

pages.title: Targeting Rules
pages.body:
# Targeting Rules

A rule predicate matches on attributes the caller supplies in the evaluation
context: plan, region, app version, or any custom key.

| Operator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `eq` / `neq` | exact match |
| `in` / `not_in` | membership in a list |
| `gte` / `lte` | numeric or semver comparison |
| `matches` | anchored regular expression |

Unknown attributes never throw — a predicate over a missing key simply does
not match, so a stale SDK cannot fail a rollout closed.

pages.title: Evaluation Engine
pages.body:
# Evaluation Engine

Evaluation is deliberately boring: no I/O, no clock, no network. The engine
takes a ruleset snapshot and a context map and returns a value plus the id of
the rule that produced it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Context --> Engine[Evaluator]
    Ruleset --> Engine
    Engine --> Value
    Engine --> Reason[Matched rule id]
```

Returning the matched rule id is what makes a surprising flag value
debuggable — the caller can see *why* it got what it got.

pages.title: Progressive Rollouts
pages.body:
# Progressive Rollouts

A rule can hand its value to a percentage of traffic instead of all of it. The
bucket is a stable hash of `(flag key, unit id)`, so a given user stays on the
same side of a 10% rollout across every request and every process.

Raising a rollout from 10% to 25% only ever *adds* units to the treatment
group; nobody is silently moved back.

pages.title: SDK Clients
pages.body:
# SDK Clients

The server is the source of truth, but evaluation happens in the client. An
SDK fetches the ruleset, caches it, and evaluates locally — so a flag check
costs a map lookup, not a round trip.

- Cached rulesets are versioned with an ETag; a poll with no change is a 304.
- A cold start with no cache falls back to each flag's compiled-in default.
- Losing the server never fails a request; it freezes the last known ruleset.

pages.title: Self-Hosting
pages.body:
# Self-Hosting

Beacon runs as two processes: an API server and Postgres. The ruleset is small
enough that a single node comfortably serves a whole fleet of SDK pollers.

```yaml
services:
  beacon:
    image: acme/beacon:latest
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://beacon@db/beacon
  db:
    image: postgres:16
```

There is no separate worker tier: rollout bucketing is computed in the SDK, so
the server only ever reads and writes flag definitions.

pages.title: API Reference
pages.body:
# API Reference

| Method | Path | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/rulesets/{env}` | fetch the current ruleset (ETag-cached) |
| `GET` | `/api/flags` | list flag definitions |
| `POST` | `/api/flags` | create a flag |
| `PATCH` | `/api/flags/{key}` | update rules or default |
| `POST` | `/api/evaluate` | server-side evaluation, for scripts |

`POST /api/evaluate` exists for callers with no SDK (a shell script, a cron
job). It runs the same evaluator the SDKs embed.

projects.desc: A small in-process task queue for Python: typed jobs, retries with backoff, and a pluggable broker.

pages.title: Overview
pages.body:
# sandbox

Sandbox is a small in-process task queue for Python. It runs typed jobs on a pool
of workers, retries failures with exponential backoff, and keeps queue state in a
pluggable broker.

## At a glance

- Jobs are plain functions registered with a decorator.
- Workers pull from one ordered queue; ordering is FIFO within a priority band.
- A broker adapter (memory, Redis, or Postgres) owns durability.

pages.title: Configuration
pages.body:
# Configuration

Sandbox reads an optional `sandbox.toml` and falls back to defaults, so an
import-and-go setup needs no configuration file at all.

```toml
[queue]
workers = 4
max_retries = 3
backoff = "exponential"

[broker]
kind = "memory"
```

Every key can be overridden by a matching `SANDBOX_*` environment variable, which
takes precedence over the file.

A self-hosted secrets and environment-variable manager for teams.
Secrets are sealed at rest and delivered at runtime through a CLI, a
REST API, and a web UI, so a service reads its config without a
plaintext `.env` ever landing on disk.
